content: The guidelines for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected adults, adolescents, and children were developed as a supplement to the 2016 consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection. These guidelines, published in March 2018 by the World Health Organization (WHO), provide evidence-based recommendations for addressing cryptococcal disease, a significant opportunistic infection among individuals with advanced HIV disease. Cryptococcal disease, primarily caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in people with advanced HIV. The most common presentation is cryptococcal meningitis, which accounts for approximately 15% of all AIDS-related deaths globally, with the majority of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2014, an estimated 223,100 cases of cryptococcal meningitis resulted in 181,100 deaths among people living with HIV. Less common presentations include pulmonary disease and involvement of the skin, lymph nodes, or bones. Cryptococcal disease is rare in children with HIV, even in regions with a high burden of the disease among adults. The guidelines emphasize the importance of early diagnosis, prevention, and effective treatment strategies. Key recommendations include: 1. Diagnosis of Cryptococcal Meningitis: This is strongly recommended for adults and adolescents, with moderate-certainty evidence, and for children, with low-certainty evidence. In settings where lumbar puncture is not immediately available or contraindicated, rapid serum, plasma, or whole-blood CrAg assays are recommended if accessible. If CrAg testing is unavailable, prompt referral for further investigation and treatment is advised. 2. Prevention and Screening: Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy is recommended for adults and adolescents with HIV who have a CD4 cell count below 100 cells/mm³. This approach aims to prevent the progression to invasive cryptococcal disease before initiating or reinitiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Screening may also be considered for individuals with a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³. In the absence of CrAg screening, fluconazole primary prophylaxis is recommended for individuals with a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³ and may be considered for those with a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³. Screening and prophylaxis are not recommended for children due to the low incidence of cryptococcal meningitis in this age group. 3. Treatment of Cryptococcal Meningitis: The preferred induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis is one week of amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day) combined with flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day in four divided doses), followed by one week of fluconazole (1200 mg/day for adults or 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents, up to a maximum of 800 mg daily). This regimen is strongly recommended for adults and adolescents (moderate-certainty evidence) and for children (low-certainty evidence). Alternative induction regimens include two weeks of fluconazole (1200 mg/day for adults or 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents) combined with flucytosine or amphotericin B combined with fluconazole. The consolidation phase involves fluconazole (800 mg/day for adults or 6–12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents, up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) for eight weeks following induction therapy. Maintenance therapy (secondary prophylaxis) with fluconazole (200 mg/day for adults or 6 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents) is recommended to prevent relapse. 4. Adjunctive Therapy: Routine use of systemic corticosteroids during the induction phase is not recommended for treating HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis due to the risk of increased mortality. 5. Timing of ART Initiation: Immediate initiation of ART is not recommended for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to the risk of increased mortality. ART should be deferred for 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment. 6. Management of Amphotericin B Toxicity: Safe administration of amphotericin B requires a minimum package of pre-emptive hydration, electrolyte replacement, and toxicity monitoring to minimize serious side effects such as hypokalemia, nephrotoxicity, and anemia. 7. The guidelines were developed using the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence and were informed by systematic reviews. They also consider resource use, cost implications, and patient and provider preferences. These recommendations are intended for HIV program managers, policymakers, healthcare professionals, and organizations supporting HIV care in resource-limited settings with a high burden of cryptococcal disease.
